Diamond
DYE-uh-muhnd
noun
Hebrew yahalom (H3095) or shamir (H8068) — a precious stone of extreme hardness, identified today as diamond or alternatively as corundum or hard quartz; the sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18; 39:11). The Hebrew shamir also describes a substance harder than flint with which God engraves the heart-tablet of Judah's sin (Jer 17:1).

Biblical Definition

Diamond is the sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18; 39:11), one of the precious stones covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13), and — most strikingly — the substance God uses to describe the engraving of Judah's sin: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars" (Jer 17:1). The Hebrew yahalom means literally "the smiter" or "the strikingly hard one" — from a root meaning to strike or hammer; the related shamir means "thorn" or "adamant" and is used three times as the harder-than-flint engraving substance (Jer 17:1; Ezek 3:9; Zech 7:12). The stone's defining feature in Scripture is its HARDNESS — its ability to inscribe or be inscribed only at great cost. Sin engraved with a diamond pen is sin engraved permanently; God's word engraved on hearts of stone (Ezek 3:9; 11:19; 36:26; Zech 7:12) is permanent in the opposite direction. The same hardness that makes the stone the perfect engraving tool for sin (Jer 17:1) becomes the perfect material of the new heart God promises His people (Ezek 36:26 — though there the heart is FLESH replacing stone, the inverse picture). The sixth stone of the breastplate, representing Issachar in many traditional reconstructions, sat in the middle row carrying that hardness over the high priest's heart — a daily reminder that what is engraved on hearts (whether sin or righteousness) is engraved permanently. In Christ, the diamond engraving of Judah's sin is overwritten by the diamond engraving of the law of God on the new heart (2 Cor 3:3; Heb 8:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

A precious stone of extreme hardness; sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate and the substance with which God engraves sin and law on the heart.

expand to see more

DIAMOND, noun. A precious stone, the hardest of all natural substances; biblical "diamond" may refer to actual diamond or to corundum (sapphire/ruby) or to other very hard stones. The defining biblical feature is hardness, especially for engraving.

In Scripture, the sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18); one of Eden's covering stones (Ezek 28:13); the substance with which Judah's sin is engraved on the heart (Jer 17:1); described elsewhere as "adamant" harder than flint (Ezek 3:9; Zech 7:12).

Key Scripture

Exodus 28:18 — "And the second row shall be an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond."

Jeremiah 17:1 — "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond: it is graven upon the table of their heart, and upon the horns of your altars."

Ezekiel 36:26 — "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh."

2 Corinthians 3:3 — "Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart."

Modern Corruption

Diamond is corrupted when its biblical engraving-function is reduced to mere preciousness (modern jewelry industry), or when the heart-engraving theology of Jeremiah 17 and 2 Corinthians 3 is severed from the breastplate-stone catalog.

expand to see more

Jewelry-industry reduction. The De Beers "a diamond is forever" advertising campaign of the twentieth century permanently lodged the diamond in Western consciousness as a luxury love-token. The biblical diamond is something far more weighty: the engraving substance with which God writes sin (and, by promise, His law) on the human heart. "A diamond is forever" is true in a far more frightening way than the ad implied — sin engraved with a diamond pen is sin engraved permanently, until the One who writes a new covenant law on a new heart removes it.

Heart-theology severance. Jeremiah 17:1 says Judah's sin is diamond-engraved on the heart. Ezekiel 36:26 promises a new heart of flesh in place of the heart of stone. 2 Corinthians 3:3 says believers are now "the epistle of Christ" written with the Spirit of the living God on the fleshly tables of the heart. The whole arc — diamond-engraved sin → stony heart removed → fleshly heart inscribed by Spirit — is the gospel in heart-engraving terms. The sixth stone of the breastplate sat over the high priest's heart as a daily testimony: hearts can only be engraved permanently, but the priest's intercession is for those whose engraving needs replacing.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yahalom (H3095) or shamir (H8068) — a precious stone of extreme hardness; the sixth stone of the high priest's breastplate.

expand to see more

Hebrew yahalom (H3095) — diamond; literally "the smiter" or "the strikingly hard one"; sixth stone of the breastplate

Hebrew shamir (H8068) — adamant/diamond; the engraving substance harder than flint (Jer 17:1; Ezek 3:9; Zech 7:12)

Defining biblical feature is HARDNESS — used for permanent engraving, whether of sin (Jer 17:1) or covenant law (Heb 8:10)

In traditional breastplate-tribe reconstructions, represents Issachar in the middle row

Usage

"Sin engraved with a diamond pen lasts forever — and only the Author of a new covenant can engrave a new heart in its place."

"The sixth stone of the breastplate was diamond — the priest carried daily over his heart the substance of permanent inscription."

"Christ engraves His law on hearts of flesh; the old diamond-cut testimony of sin is replaced by the diamond-permanence of grace."
